    For n = 1,000 that's 499,500 pairs.

0.9 Orthonormal matrices and the SVD

blocks.html:
• The ideaThe SVD separates a matrix into three operations: rotate, stretch along the axes, rotate again.
  • That decomposition is the singular value decomposition.

blocks.html:
• An orthonormal (orthogonal) matrix Q has Q⊤Q=I.

    It is a rotation (possibly with a reflection): it never changes lengths, ∥Qu∥=∥u∥.

    Their squares σi2​ are the eigenvalues of MM⊤.

sections.title: Preserving all pairs: the final JL guarantee

blocks.text: Learning goal: Choose a target dimension that preserves every pair with high probability.
Conditions and notation

Use both tails and the union bound; pair failures need not be independent.

• The ideaOne coin lands heads with probability ½, but two coins both landing heads is only ¼.

  • The union bound adds up all the small failure chances, and because each one is exponentially small, k only needs to grow like log n to pay for all of them.

sections.title: The SVD interpretation of random projection

blocks.text: Learning goal: Understand projection as orthogonal changes of coordinates and scaling.
Conditions and notation
For the displayed k × d SVD, assume k ≤ d.
Squared singular values are eigenvalues of MMᵀ.
Random directions are uniform in every dimension; nearly equal singular values need a suitable dimension ratio.

blocks.html:
• The ideaSo far we treated M as a source of random measurements and estimated a length from them.
  • Now look at M as a machine.
  • The SVD uses orthogonal changes of coordinates and scaling.
  • For a random Gaussian M, the first rotation is random, so it can't favour any direction of your vector.
  • All k stretches are about equal, so nothing gets crushed.
  • The last rotation doesn't change length at all.
  • Result: the length comes out roughly unchanged.

Random rotation and scaling: the key facts
For a fixed unit input vector, the first orthogonal transformation produces a random unit direction in d dimensions.
